questions.q: Which of these best describes 'weather' as the chapter defines it?
questions.a: Weather is the state of the Earth's atmosphere at a particular time and place.
o: The state of the Earth's atmosphere at a particular time and place
The layer of gases that surrounds the Earth
The amount of water vapour present in the air
Any form of water that falls from the sky

questions.q: In which layer of the Earth's atmosphere do almost all weather phenomena take place?
questions.a: The troposphere, the layer closest to the surface of the Earth.

questions.q: A notice board in a Bhubaneswar school reads: 'Today: 18 degrees Celsius, 1009 mb, wind 12 km/h, relative humidity 68%.' Which information about the weather has the notice left out?
questions.a: Precipitation, and the direction of the wind: the notice gives temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind speed and humidity, but says nothing about rain, snow, sleet or hail, and wind is described by both its speed and its direction.
o: Precipitation and the direction of the wind
Atmospheric pressure and the direction of the wind

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the atmosphere and weather.
I. Almost all weather phenomena take place in the stratosphere, the layer above the troposphere.
II. Atmospheric pressure is the amount of water vapour present in the air.
III. Sleet, which is frozen or partly frozen rain, is a form of precipitation.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: III only: statement I is wrong because almost all weather phenomena take place in the troposphere, the layer closest to the Earth's surface; statement II is wrong because atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air above us, felt on the Earth's surface, while the amount of water vapour in the air is humidity.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Snow and hail are both counted as precipitation.
Reason (R): Precipitation is any form of water, such as rain, snow, sleet or hail, that falls from the sky.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: snow and hail are forms of water falling from the sky, which is what precipitation means.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: Water vapour, whose amount in the air is called humidity, is water in a gaseous form and not in a liquid form. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: True. Water vapour is water in gaseous instead of liquid form, and humidity is the amount of this water vapour present in the air.
s: Reason: water vapour is water in gaseous, not liquid, form; humidity is the amount of it in the air

questions.q: (a) What is humidity? (b) Name one form of precipitation other than rain.
questions.a: (a) Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. (b) Any one of snow, sleet or hail.
s: (a) The amount of water vapour in the air

questions.q: Name the element of weather described in each line. (a) How hot or cold the atmosphere is. (b) The weight of the air above us, felt on the Earth's surface. (c) The movement of air, including its speed and direction.
questions.a: (a) Temperature. (b) Atmospheric pressure. (c) Wind.

questions.q:
Students in Dehradun pinned this note on their class board one January morning: 'Temperature 9 degrees Celsius. 4 mm of sleet has collected in the gauge since 6 a.m. Barometer 1008 mb. Air very still; not a leaf moves. The air feels damp.' A pen-friend in Chennai wants to compare her own weather with theirs.
(a) Which element of weather does the reading 1008 mb describe?
(b) Which entry describes precipitation, and why does it count as precipitation?
(c) Name the two elements that the note records only in words, without any number.
(d) Explain why the pen-friend can compare the temperature entry with her own weather but cannot properly compare 'the air feels damp'.
questions.a: (a) Atmospheric pressure. (b) The sleet entry: sleet is frozen or partly frozen rain, and precipitation is any form of water that falls from the sky. (c) Wind ('air very still') and humidity ('the air feels damp'). (d) The temperature is given on a commonly agreed scale, degrees Celsius, so it means the same to both of them; 'feels damp' is a personal feeling that differs from person to person, so it cannot be compared without a measured figure.
s: (b) Sleet, because it is water falling from the sky
(d) Celsius is a common standard; 'damp' is a personal feeling with no common measure

questions.q: A weather balloon carrying a thermometer rises to 12 kilometres above the ground. Riya says, 'At 12 km the balloon is always still inside the troposphere, wherever in the world it is launched.' Check her claim for a launch near the poles and for a launch in the tropical zone.
questions.a: Riya's claim is not correct. The troposphere extends to a height of 6 to 18 km. Near the poles, where the cold air contracts, it is less thick, so a balloon at 12 km may already be above it. In the tropical zone, where the warm air expands, it is thicker, so a balloon at 12 km is still inside it. The answer depends on where the balloon is launched.
s: States that the troposphere extends 6 to 18 km
Near the poles the layer is thinner, so 12 km may lie above it
In the tropical zone it is thicker, so 12 km is inside it; the claim 'always' is rejected

questions.q: What is meteorology?
questions.a: Meteorology is the systematic study of weather and its evolution; it is the basis for weather forecasting.
o: The systematic study of weather and its evolution
The study of the rocks beneath the Earth's surface
The study of the stars and planets
The collecting of weather sayings from elders

questions.q: Which of these is one of nature's signals that the chapter says people have observed to forecast rain or storms?
questions.a: Frogs croaking loudly. The chapter speaks of birds flying low, ants carrying eggs to higher ground and pine cones closing in humid air, so the other three choices reverse those signs.
o: Birds flying very high in the sky
Ants carrying their eggs to lower ground
Pine cones staying wide open all day

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I: 1. Squirrels gathering nuts  2. Hail  3. Meteorologists  4. A commonly agreed way to measure temperature
Column II: (a) Use precise measurements to predict how the weather of a region will behave after hours, days or weeks  (b) Lets Krishnan in Chennai tell Amir in Kashmir exactly how cold it is  (c) One of Nature's signals that people have read to forecast coming rain or storms  (d) Small, hard balls of ice that fall from the sky like rain
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: squirrels gathering nuts is one of Nature's signals of coming rain or storms; hail is small, hard balls of ice that fall from the sky like rain; meteorologists use measurements to predict a region's weather hours, days or weeks ahead; a common measure lets Krishnan convey to Amir how cold Chennai is.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Tenzin in Leh texts his cousin in Kolkata, 'It is very cold here today.' From this message alone, his cousin cannot tell how cold Leh is.
Reason (R): Every person feels a given temperature as equally cold.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: what feels cold to one person may feel quite pleasant to another, which is exactly why a commonly agreed measure of temperature is needed.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: A pine cone that is wide open shows that the air around it is humid. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: False. Pine cones open in dry conditions to release their seeds; they close in humid conditions to protect them.
s: Reason: cones open in dry air and close in humid air

questions.q: (a) What does the word 'forecast' mean? (b) Name any two natural signs that people have observed to forecast rain or storms.
questions.a: (a) To predict or find out in advance, here the weather. (b) Any two of: birds flying low, ants carrying eggs to higher ground, squirrels gathering nuts, frogs croaking loudly, the opening and closing of pine cones.
s: (a) To predict or find out in advance

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) What do ants do that indicates an expected change in the weather, especially heavy rain? (b) How has people's knowledge of nature's weather signs reached us today? (c) For which yearly event do people in many parts of India still use traditional ways to predict the weather?
questions.a: (a) They shift (carry) their eggs to higher ground. (b) It has been passed down from generation to generation. (c) The arrival of the monsoon.
s: (a) Ants shift their eggs to higher ground
(b) Passed down from generation to generation

questions.q: Gangamma predicts rain from frogs croaking loudly. A meteorologist at the district weather office predicts rain from instrument readings. Give one way in which their work is alike and two ways in which it differs.
questions.a: Alike: both observe the world around them to forecast the weather in advance. Differences (any two): the meteorologist measures the elements of weather with instruments, while Gangamma reads natural signs; the meteorologist's readings use common standards and are precise, so they can be compared between places; the meteorologist can predict a few hours, days or even weeks ahead, while Gangamma relies on knowledge passed down through generations.
s: One correct likeness: both forecast the weather from observation

questions.q: Four pen-friends in Shimla, Chennai, Jaipur and Guwahati each describe today's weather in one word, such as 'chilly', 'pleasant' or 'sticky'. Their teacher says the four words cannot be compared. (a) The Shimla and Chennai friends both wrote 'chilly', but their thermometers read 12 and 24 degrees Celsius. By how many degrees did the two 'chilly' mornings differ, and what does this show about one-word descriptions? (b) In what unit, and with which instrument, should each of them report temperature? (c) In what unit, and with which instrument, should each report rainfall? (d) The Guwahati friend wrote 'sticky' and the Jaipur friend 'pleasant'; their hygrometers read 78% and 30% relative humidity. Using the chapter's ranges, say what kind of air each word was really describing.
questions.a: (a) 24 - 12 = 12 degrees Celsius. The same word was used for two very different temperatures, so a word is only a personal feeling and gives no commonly agreed measure that can be compared. (b) Degrees Celsius, read from a thermometer. (c) Millimetres, read from a rain gauge. (d) 78% lies in the humid range of 60% to 80%, so 'sticky' described humid air; 30% lies in the dry range of 20% to 40%, so 'pleasant' described dry air.
s: (a) Difference of 12 degrees Celsius, and the same word covers different temperatures, so words cannot be compared
(d) 78% is humid (60% to 80%) and 30% is dry (20% to 40%)

questions.q:
For a project, Arjun hangs a pine cone beside the school hygrometer in Ooty and notes both at noon for five days, to see whether Nature's old signal agrees with the instrument.
Monday: 32%, cone open. Tuesday: 38%, cone open. Wednesday: 71%, cone closed. Thursday: 78%, cone closed. Friday: 45%, cone open.
(a) On which days was the air humid, using the chapter's range for humid weather?
(b) Does the cone behave as the chapter says it should? Support your answer from the data.
(c) What does the cone protect by closing?
(d) Arjun says, 'The cone can replace the hygrometer.' Do you agree? Support your answer by naming the two days whose humidity differed the most although the cone looked the same, and by how much.
questions.a: (a) Wednesday (71%) and Thursday (78%), which lie in the humid range of 60% to 80%. (b) Yes: it closed on both humid days and stayed open on the drier days (32%, 38% and 45%). (c) Its seeds. (d) No. The cone only shows open or closed: it was open on Monday (32%), Tuesday (38%) and Friday (45%), yet Monday and Friday differ by 45 - 32 = 13 percentage points, more than any other pair with the same cone state (the closed days differ by only 78 - 71 = 7). The cone gives no number that can be compared with other places.
s: (b) Yes, closed on humid days and open on drier days, with data
(d) Disagrees: Monday and Friday, both open, differ by 13 percentage points; the cone gives no measured value

questions.q: In which year was the India Meteorological Department set up?
questions.a: The India Meteorological Department was set up in 1875.

questions.q: A thermometer in Bikaner shows a maximum of 35 degrees Celsius and a minimum of 18 degrees Celsius for one day. What is the range of temperature for that day?
questions.a: 17 degrees Celsius, because range = maximum - minimum = 35 - 18 = 17.

questions.q: On a day in Kohima the maximum temperature was 31 degrees Celsius and the minimum was 19 degrees Celsius. What was the mean daily temperature?
questions.a: 25 degrees Celsius, because mean daily temperature = (31 + 19) / 2 = 25.

questions.q: A science club must log the temperature every 10 minutes for a whole week and compare readings very precisely. Which thermometer suits this job best, according to the chapter?
questions.a: A digital thermometer, because the chapter says digital thermometers are more precise and can record more data.
o: A digital thermometer, because it is more precise and can record more data
A coloured-liquid thermometer, because its liquid expands when heated
A thermometer that records only the day's maximum and minimum
A clinical thermometer, because it is used to check body temperature

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A temperature of 15 degrees Celsius and a temperature of 59 degrees Fahrenheit are equally cool.
Reason (R): Celsius and Fahrenheit are two different scales for measuring temperature, and 15 degrees Celsius is the same as 59 degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the two readings are the same temperature written on two different scales.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: On a day with a maximum of 30 degrees Celsius and a minimum of 18 degrees Celsius, the mean daily temperature is 12 degrees Celsius. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. 12 degrees Celsius is the range (30 - 18). The mean daily temperature is (30 + 18) / 2 = 24 degrees Celsius.
s: Shows 12 is the range and the mean is (30 + 18) / 2 = 24 degrees Celsius

questions.q: On a winter day in Pune the maximum temperature was 27 degrees Celsius and the minimum was 13 degrees Celsius. Find (a) the range of temperature and (b) the mean daily temperature.
questions.a: (a) Range = 27 - 13 = 14 degrees Celsius. (b) Mean daily temperature = (27 + 13) / 2 = 20 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Lata compares two days in Raipur. Day A: maximum 38, minimum 22 degrees Celsius. Day B: maximum 33, minimum 25 degrees Celsius. She says, 'Day B was warmer on the whole and its temperature also changed less during the day, because its minimum was higher.' (a) Find the mean daily temperature of each day. (b) Find the range of each day. (c) Check each half of Lata's claim using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Day A: (38 + 22) / 2 = 30 degrees Celsius; Day B: (33 + 25) / 2 = 29 degrees Celsius. (b) Day A: 38 - 22 = 16 degrees Celsius; Day B: 33 - 25 = 8 degrees Celsius. (c) The first half is wrong: the mean uses both the maximum and the minimum, and Day A's maximum was 5 degrees higher while Day B's minimum was only 3 degrees higher, so Day A had the higher mean (30 against 29 degrees Celsius). The second half is right: Day B's range (8) is smaller than Day A's (16), so its temperature changed less during the day. A higher minimum alone settles neither half; the mean and the range do.
s: (c) First half rejected (Day A's mean is higher); second half accepted (Day B's range is smaller)

questions.q:
A weather station in Jodhpur recorded these (maximum, minimum) temperatures in degrees Celsius for one week in May: Mon (40, 26), Tue (42, 27), Wed (43, 29), Thu (41, 25), Fri (39, 24), Sat (44, 27), Sun (42, 26).
(a) Give the highest maximum and the lowest minimum of the week.
(b) Find the range of temperature for the whole week.
(c) Which day had the largest daily range? Show the range.
(d) Find the mean daily temperature of each day.
(e) By how many degrees is the range for the whole week greater than Saturday's daily range? Explain why the week's range can never be smaller than the range of any one day in it.
questions.a: (a) Highest maximum 44 degrees Celsius (Saturday); lowest minimum 24 degrees Celsius (Friday). (b) Range for the week = 44 - 24 = 20 degrees Celsius. (c) Saturday: 44 - 27 = 17 degrees Celsius (the other days have 14 to 16). (d) Mon 33, Tue 34.5, Wed 36, Thu 33, Fri 31.5, Sat 35.5, Sun 34 degrees Celsius. (e) 20 - 17 = 3 degrees Celsius. The week's range uses the highest maximum and the lowest minimum of all seven days, so it is at least as large as the gap between any one day's maximum and minimum.
s: (e) 3 degrees Celsius, with the reason that the week uses the highest maximum and lowest minimum

questions.q:
The weather club of a school in Shillong reads its maximum-minimum thermometer every evening and writes the readings on a chart.
Day 1: maximum 21, minimum 11 degrees Celsius.
Day 2: maximum 23, minimum 12 degrees Celsius.
Day 3: maximum 20, minimum 14 degrees Celsius.
(a) What was the maximum temperature on Day 2?
(b) Find the range of temperature on Day 1.
(c) Find the mean daily temperature on Day 3.
(d) Which day had the smallest range of temperature?
questions.a: (a) 23 degrees Celsius. (b) 21 - 11 = 10 degrees Celsius. (c) (20 + 14) / 2 = 17 degrees Celsius. (d) Day 3, with a range of 6 degrees Celsius (Day 1 had 10 and Day 2 had 11).

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure atmospheric pressure?
questions.a: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, usually in millibars.

questions.q: After a shower, the water collected in a school's rain gauge stands 8 mm high on its scale. How much rainfall did the area receive?
questions.a: 8 mm of rainfall, because the height of the water collected in the gauge is the rainfall.

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I: 1. Normal atmospheric pressure at the sea coast  2. A pressure that indicates a depression  3. Usual pressure at Khardung La in Ladakh  4. Unit generally shown by barometers
Column II: (a) Around 1013 mb  (b) Below 1000 mb  (c) About 650 mb  (d) Millibar
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d: normal coastal pressure is around 1013 mb, below 1000 mb indicates a depression, Khardung La has about 650 mb, and barometers display millibars.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): People who journey to places at a high altitude are advised to make pauses on the way up.
Reason (R): The air at high altitude is thinner and holds less oxygen, so the body needs time to acclimatise to the new condition.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because the thinner air at altitude gives the lungs less oxygen, pauses on the way up allow the body to acclimatise.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
I. People may feel breathless at high altitudes because less oxygen gets into their lungs and blood.
II. A barometer at a coastal town that reads 1008 mb indicates a depression.
III. Air pressure on a mountain top is lower than on the plain below, because the air there is thinner.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only: thinner air on a mountain means lower pressure and less oxygen, so people may feel breathless. II is wrong because only a pressure below 1000 mb indicates a depression; 1008 mb is a little below the coast's normal 1013 mb but still above 1000 mb.

questions.q: True or False: Although there are several types of barometers, their readings can usually be compared with one another. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. Barometers generally display atmospheric pressure in the same unit, the millibar (mb), so a reading such as 1013 mb means the same pressure whichever type of barometer shows it.
s: Reason: barometers generally display the same unit, the millibar

questions.q: (a) Name the instrument used to measure rainfall. (b) Name the part of it that catches the rain and the part in which the rainwater is collected.
questions.a: (a) Rain gauge. (b) The funnel catches the rain and the cylinder (measuring tube) collects it.

questions.q: A rain gauge in a Konkan village gave these daily readings for one week: Mon 12 mm, Tue 0 mm, Wed 25 mm, Thu 7 mm, Fri 0 mm, Sat 18 mm, Sun 8 mm. (a) Find the total rainfall for the week. (b) Find the average daily rainfall. (c) Name the two wettest days and show that together they gave more than half of the week's rain.
questions.a: (a) 12 + 0 + 25 + 7 + 0 + 18 + 8 = 70 mm. (b) 70 / 7 = 10 mm. (c) Wednesday (25 mm) and Saturday (18 mm): together 25 + 18 = 43 mm, which is more than half of 70 mm (35 mm).
s: (c) Wednesday and Saturday, 43 mm, more than 35 mm

questions.q: A school in Mysuru keeps a rain gauge on an open, flat platform. (a) Name the instrument. (b) Why should it stand on a flat surface? (c) Why should it be placed in an open area, away from trees and walls? (d) The readings for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday are 15 mm, 9 mm and 12 mm. Find the total. (e) Find the average daily rainfall for these three days.
questions.a: (a) Rain gauge. (b) So that it will not tilt or topple with the wind. (c) So that no object obstructs the rain from falling into it. (d) 15 + 9 + 12 = 36 mm. (e) 36 / 3 = 12 mm.
s: (b) So it does not tilt or topple

questions.q:
A district officer compares weekly rainfall, measured with rain gauges, in two villages during July.
Village A: Week 1, 42 mm; Week 2, 0 mm; Week 3, 15 mm; Week 4, 3 mm.
Village B: Week 1, 10 mm; Week 2, 12 mm; Week 3, 14 mm; Week 4, 11 mm.
(a) Find the total July rainfall in each village.
(b) Find the average weekly rainfall in each village.
(c) Which village had the steadier rain from week to week? Support your answer with the data.
(d) A farmer says, 'Village A got more rain, so its crops never went short of water in July.' Judge this claim.
questions.a: (a) Village A: 60 mm; Village B: 47 mm. (b) Village A: 60 / 4 = 15 mm; Village B: 47 / 4 = 11.75 mm. (c) Village B: its weeks lay between 10 and 14 mm, while Village A's ranged from 0 to 42 mm. (d) The claim is not justified: Village A had more rain in total, but Week 2 had no rain at all and Week 4 only 3 mm, so its crops may well have gone short; the total hides the dry weeks.
s: (c) Village B, weeks 10 to 14 mm against 0 to 42 mm
(d) Rejects the claim using the 0 mm and 3 mm weeks

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure humidity?
questions.a: A hygrometer measures humidity.

questions.q:
Match each instrument in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Wind sock  2. Anemometer  3. Hygrometer  4. Wind vane
Column II: (a) Shows pilots the wind direction during take-off and landing  (b) Has metal cups that spin to give the wind speed in km/h  (c) Measures relative humidity  (d) Has a pointer that turns in the direction of the wind
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d: the wind sock on the tarmac guides pilots, the anemometer's cups give wind speed, the hygrometer measures humidity and the wind vane's pointer turns in the direction of the wind.

questions.q: A hygrometer in Jaisalmer reads a relative humidity of 30%. How would the chapter describe this air?
questions.a: Dry weather, because dry weather has a relative humidity between 20% and 40%.
o: Air with no water vapour at all

questions.q: On the same afternoon, at the same temperature, hygrometers read: Town P 25%, Town Q 48%, Town R 66%, Town S 92%. In which town will sweat on the skin evaporate most slowly?
questions.a: Town S: it has the most water vapour already in the air (92%), and when humidity is high, water evaporates slowly.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Air with a relative humidity of 0% is not found in natural conditions.
Reason (R): Air with a relative humidity of 100% is saturated with water vapour.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the chapter says air with no water vapour at all (0%) is impossible in nature, and that saturated air is 100%, but the second fact does not explain the first.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
I. The cups of an anemometer rotate more slowly when the wind is stronger.
II. In a wind vane, the wind pushes the tail and the pointer turns in the direction of the wind.
III. Humidity depends only on temperature, and not on wind, pressure or location.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: II only: statement I is wrong because the stronger the wind, the faster the cups rotate; statement III is wrong because humidity depends on temperature, wind, pressure and location.

questions.q: (a) Why do museums monitor humidity? (b) Name one industrial process in which measuring humidity is important.
questions.a: (a) Museums need to keep a dry environment to preserve their exhibits. (b) Food processing.
s: (a) To keep a dry environment that preserves the exhibits

questions.q: On a day with the same temperature in both places, Place P has a relative humidity of 35% and a strong wind, while Place Q has 78% and very still air. (a) Classify the air at each place as dry or humid, using the chapter's ranges. (b) At which place will wet clothes dry faster? Give two reasons. (c) At which place is a person likely to sweat more?
questions.a: (a) Place P is dry (dry weather is 20% to 40%); Place Q is humid (humid weather is 60% to 80%). (b) Place P: water evaporates faster when the air holds less water vapour, and a greater wind speed dries things faster (the chapter notes that a greater wind speed makes the soil dry faster). (c) Place Q, where the humid air lets sweat evaporate only slowly.
s: (a) P dry, Q humid, with the ranges
(b) P, with both reasons: lower humidity, and stronger wind dries faster (as it dries the soil faster)

questions.q: A sailing club on a lake needs a day for its beginners' race. The wind speed must be between 10 and 20 km/h, and the club wants the relative humidity below 60% so that the sails dry before they are packed away. The forecast gives: Mon 8 km/h, 45%; Tue 14 km/h, 72%; Wed 27 km/h, 50%; Thu 18 km/h, 55%; Fri 12 km/h, 66%. (a) Which days meet the wind rule? (b) Which days meet the humidity rule? (c) Which day should the club choose? (d) Name the instruments that give the wind speed and the humidity.
questions.a: (a) Tuesday (14 km/h), Thursday (18 km/h) and Friday (12 km/h). (b) Monday (45%), Wednesday (50%) and Thursday (55%). (c) Thursday, the only day that meets both rules. (d) The anemometer gives the wind speed and the hygrometer gives the humidity.

questions.q:
During a geography lesson on humidity, the class opens a weather website. On one afternoon the website shows the relative humidity in four cities: Kochi 78%, Mangaluru 74%, Jaipur 28% and Shimla 55%. Before looking, Farah had guessed that Kochi would be more humid than Jaipur because Kochi is near the sea.
(a) Which city has air in the chapter's dry-weather range?
(b) Which cities have air in the humid-weather range?
(c) Does the data support Farah's guess? By how many percentage points do the two cities differ?
(d) A pickle maker needs air in the dry-weather range to sun-dry mango slices. Which city suits him, and why does Shimla not suit him?
questions.a: (a) Jaipur (28% lies between 20% and 40%). (b) Kochi (78%) and Mangaluru (74%), which lie between 60% and 80%. (c) Yes: Kochi has 78% and Jaipur 28%, a difference of 50 percentage points. (d) Jaipur; Shimla's 55% is above the dry range of 20% to 40%, so its air is not dry enough.
s: (c) Supports the guess; difference 50 percentage points
(d) Jaipur; Shimla's 55% is above the dry range

questions.q: What does an Automated Weather Station (AWS) do?
questions.a: It uses sensors to measure and record weather data, such as temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation and pressure, without the need for human intervention.
o: It uses sensors to measure and record weather data without human intervention
It predicts the weather only from nature's signs
It measures only temperature and rainfall
It needs an observer to read each instrument every hour

questions.q: (a) What does a weather station do? (b) Why are its readings taken at regular intervals?
questions.a: (a) It brings together all the instruments needed to measure the weather at a place, making it easy to measure and track the weather. (b) Regular readings help in mapping and forecasting the weather.
s: (a) Brings the weather instruments together at one place
(b) Helps in mapping and forecasting the weather

questions.q: Two coastal districts receive forecasts on the same morning. For District P, stormy weather is expected at sea, but no cyclone is expected. For District Q, a cyclone is expected to reach its coast. Which plan best matches the uses of forecasts given in the chapter?
questions.a: District P warns its fishermen not to venture out to sea, while District Q warns its fishermen and also prepares to evacuate its coastal area: the chapter says fishermen are warned when stormy weather is expected at sea, and an entire coastal area might have to be evacuated if a cyclone is expected.
o: P warns its fishermen not to go out to sea; Q warns its fishermen and also prepares to evacuate its coastal area
P prepares to evacuate its coastal area; Q only warns its fishermen not to go out to sea
Both districts evacuate their entire coastal areas at once, since any storm at sea is a cyclone
Neither district acts until its barometer has stayed below 1000 mb for a whole day

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A district that receives an accurate forecast of very heavy rain three days ahead can reduce the harm the rain does.
Reason (R): Accurate predictions enable local governments to mobilise resources and prepare for disasters before they happen.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the three days' warning lets the local government mobilise resources and prepare, which is why the harm can be reduced.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
I. In 2023 the National Disaster Management Authority set up an AWS at a glacial lake in Sikkim.
II. That station stands at an altitude of more than 4800 metres above sea level.
III. An Automated Weather Station needs a person to read each instrument and write down the data.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only: statement III is wrong because an AWS is self-operating; its sensors measure and record the data without the need for human intervention.

questions.q: True or False: A weather office that opened last week can already forecast as reliably as an office that has recorded data for ten years, as long as both use the same instruments. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Meteorologists predict the weather by collecting data with instruments over long periods of time and studying it with scientific methods. Having the same instruments is not enough: one week of readings is far too short a record to study, while the older office has ten years of data to work from.
s: Reason: forecasting needs data collected over long periods and studied; one week's record is too short even with the same instruments

questions.q: A school wants to set up its own weather station. Name the instruments it needs to measure: (a) rainfall and atmospheric pressure; (b) wind direction and wind speed; (c) temperature and humidity.
questions.a: (a) A rain gauge and a barometer. (b) A wind vane for the direction and an anemometer for the speed. (c) A thermometer and a hygrometer.

questions.q:
The weather office issues a five-day forecast for a district of Rajasthan, in degrees Celsius. Day 1: max 44, min 29. Day 2: max 46, min 31. Day 3: max 47, min 30. Day 4: max 45, min 28. Day 5: max 42, min 27. The district shortens school hours on every day whose maximum is 45 degrees Celsius or above.
(a) Which is the hottest day? Find its mean daily temperature.
(b) Find the range of temperature on Day 3 and on Day 5. On which of the two days does the temperature change more?
(c) On how many of the five days will school hours be shortened? Name them.
(d) Using the chapter, explain how receiving this forecast before Day 1 helps the local government.
questions.a: (a) Day 3, with the highest maximum of 47 degrees Celsius; mean = (47 + 30) / 2 = 38.5 degrees Celsius. (b) Day 3: 47 - 30 = 17 degrees Celsius; Day 5: 42 - 27 = 15 degrees Celsius; the temperature changes more on Day 3. (c) Three days: Day 2 (46), Day 3 (47) and Day 4 (45); Day 4 counts because 45 is 'or above', while Day 1 (44) and Day 5 (42) do not. (d) Accurate predictions in advance enable the local government to mobilise resources and prepare, for example by arranging drinking water and announcing the new school timings before the hot days arrive.
s: (b) Ranges 17 and 15 degrees Celsius; more change on Day 3
(d) Advance forecast lets the government mobilise resources and prepare before the event

questions.q:
A town's weather station recorded this for five days. Mon: max 33, min 24 degrees Celsius, rain 0 mm, 1010 mb, wind 12 km/h, humidity 58%. Tue: 31, 23, rain 22 mm, 1004 mb, wind 18 km/h, 79%. Wed: 34, 25, rain 0 mm, 1011 mb, wind 24 km/h, 62%. Thu: 30, 22, rain 4 mm, 998 mb, wind 35 km/h, 76%. Fri: 32, 22, rain 0 mm, 1012 mb, wind 14 km/h, 46%. A school plans a midday nature walk next week and assumes that next week's weather will repeat this record. Its rule: no rain, no depression and wind below 20 km/h; among the days that pass, choose the one with the lowest mean daily temperature.
(a) Which days had no rain?
(b) On which day did the pressure indicate a depression? Explain.
(c) Which of the dry days had wind below 20 km/h?
(d) Find the mean daily temperature of each dry day.
(e) If next week's weather repeats this record, which day should the school choose? Show how the rule picks it.
questions.a: (a) Monday, Wednesday and Friday. (b) Thursday: 998 mb is below 1000 mb, which indicates a depression. (c) Monday (12 km/h) and Friday (14 km/h); Wednesday's wind was 24 km/h. (d) Monday (33 + 24) / 2 = 28.5, Wednesday (34 + 25) / 2 = 29.5 and Friday (32 + 22) / 2 = 27 degrees Celsius. (e) Friday. Only Monday and Friday pass all three conditions (no rain, pressure 1000 mb or more, wind below 20 km/h); of these, Friday has the lower mean daily temperature, 27 against 28.5 degrees Celsius.
s: (e) Friday: only Monday and Friday pass, and Friday's mean (27) is lower than Monday's (28.5)

questions.q:
A farmers' cooperative near Nashik reads its Automated Weather Station every evening before planning the next day's work in the grape fields. Day 1: rain 18 mm, wind 8 km/h, relative humidity 78%. Day 2: rain 0 mm, wind 10 km/h, 70%. Day 3: rain 0 mm, wind 32 km/h, 34%. Day 4: rain 0 mm, wind 26 km/h, 38%.
(a) On which days was the air in the chapter's dry-weather range?
(b) By how many km/h did the wind speed rise from Day 2 to Day 3?
(c) On which day would the soil have dried fastest? Give two reasons from the data.
(d) A member says, 'Day 4 was drier than Day 2 because no rain fell on Day 4.' Is the conclusion right? Is the reason right? Use the data.
questions.a: (a) Day 3 (34%) and Day 4 (38%), which lie between 20% and 40%. (b) 32 - 10 = 22 km/h. (c) Day 3: it had the greatest wind speed (32 km/h), and a greater wind speed makes the soil dry faster; its air was also the driest (34%), so water evaporates faster. (d) The conclusion is right but the reason is wrong. Day 4's air (38%) was in the dry-weather range, while Day 2's (70%) was in the humid range of 60% to 80%, so Day 4 was drier. But no rain fell on Day 2 either, so 'no rain' cannot be the difference; the difference is the amount of water vapour in the air, shown by the humidity.
s: (c) Day 3: strongest wind and driest air
(d) Conclusion right (38% dry against 70% humid); reason wrong, since Day 2 also had no rain
